figures.caption: Fig. 1: LEveled Gaussian splatting for Open-vocabulary scene understanding (LEGO). By parsing scenes into a unified, level-wise semantic hierarchy, LEGO establishes a robust foundation for multi-granular open-vocabulary understanding, seamlessly enabling automatic decomposition and context-aware spatial reasoning.

Fig. 2: Comparison of 3D hierarchical segmentation paradigms. (a) 2D Granularity-based methods lift view-dependent masks, leading to inconsistent 3D hierarchies across different camera distances (e.g ., petals in a nearby view vs. a whole bud in a distant view). (b) 3D Scale-based methods rely on absolute physical sizes, suffering from a semantic-scale gap. Due to intra-class scale variance, a single scale parameter may over-segment a large flower into petals while keeping smaller ones intact. (c) Our 3D Level-based paradigm automatically discovers a stable and consistent semantic hierarchy, grouping entities by their true structural compositional rank (e.g ., flowerpot → bouquet → bud) regardless of viewing distance or absolute physical size.

Fig. 3: LEGO pipeline. (a) LEGO first lifts multiview SAM masks into a 3D coherent scale space to assign them view-consistent structural levels (Sec. 3.1). (b) Guided by these level-masks, a hierarchical contrastive distillation process optimizes the decoupled identity features of the Gaussian field (Sec. 3.2).

Fig. 4: Illustration of mask level assignment. Our mechanism discovers the complete 3D hierarchical structure implicit in multi-view 2D masks, assigning each mask to its corresponding view-consistent level.

Fig. 5: Visualization of automatic hierarchical scene decomposition. Benefiting from our level-wise design, LEGO captures arbitrarily deep hierarchical structures. Here, selected entities are progressively parsed into extreme fine-grained sub-parts, while maintaining strict structural nestedness across multiple levels.
Table 3: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding results on LERF-OVS dataset.
Table 4: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding results on Mip-NeRF 360 dataset.

Fig. 6: Open-vocabulary segmentation results. While other methods struggle with severe feature blurring, LEGO cleanly isolates extremely fine-grained entities like “corn” and “onion segments”, and preserves exquisite boundaries for “LEGO bonsai”.
Fig. 7: Visualization of graph-based Chain-of-Retrieval. Colored words match bounding boxes, illustrating how coarser anchors guide fine-grained localization.
Table 7: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding results on 3D-OVS dataset.
Fig. 8: Additional promptable segmentation results in different scenes.

Fig. 9: Additional open-vocabulary segmentation results in Kitchen and Counter scene. LEGO demonstrates superior robustness in highly cluttered environments. It accurately isolates the “yellow desk” from a visually similar background wall, and successfully segments “plate” and all five “onions”.

Fig. 10: Additional open-vocabulary segmentation results in Figurines and Room scene. LEGO cleanly segments extremely fine-grained component “pirate hat”, and yields the most complete regions for “wooden floor”. Remarkably, it even retrieves unannotated “table” behind the sofa.

Fig. 12: Additional LLM-based chain of retrieval (CoR) results. LEGO accurately grounds corresponding functional sub-parts (e.g ., lights, wheels, hood) via language, demonstrating robust semantic understanding across a massive real-world truck and a miniature LEGO bulldozer.

Fig. 13: Additional LLM-based chain of retrieval (CoR) results. Our method successfully handles extreme scale variations and complex queries. It localizes tiny objects (e.g ., ground lights), resolves deep nested semantics (e.g ., flowerpot → dried flowers → sphere vine), and distinguishes specific sub-parts of plush bear and sheep.
Fig. 14: Additional open-vocabulary segmentation results in Bed, Bench, Lawn, Room and Sofa scenes of the 3D-OVS dataset.
